content: 1. Avoid unnecessary treatment, especially in areas with lower rates of HIV transmission. 2. If the second nucleic acid test (NAT) is negative, a third NAT should be performed before discontinuing antiretroviral therapy (ART). 3. For children who were never breastfed, additional testing after a negative NAT at 4–6 weeks is included in the algorithm to account for potential false-negative results. 4. If an infant shows signs and symptoms of HIV disease but NAT is unavailable, consider initiating ART, particularly if an antibody test conducted at 9 months or later is positive. 5. A dried blood spot (DBS) specimen must be collected before starting treatment to allow for later NAT testing to confirm the HIV diagnosis, as interpreting diagnostic tests while on ART can be challenging. 6. If an infant presents with signs and symptoms of HIV disease, ART should be considered while awaiting NAT results. However, another DBS specimen should be collected prior to starting treatment for later confirmation of the diagnosis. 7. Regular and periodic monitoring should be ensured while waiting for NAT availability or for antibody testing to be conducted at 18 months. Infants with signs and symptoms of HIV disease should be managed as previously described. 8. The risk of HIV transmission persists as long as breastfeeding continues. If antibody testing is conducted earlier than 3 months after breastfeeding cessation, infections acquired during the final days of breastfeeding may be missed, necessitating retesting at 18 months for final HIV status assessment. 9. If breastfeeding extends beyond 18 months, the final HIV status can only be assessed at the end of breastfeeding. If breastfeeding ends before 18 months, final diagnosis with antibody testing can only be assessed at 18 months. 10. Antibody testing should be performed at least 3 months after breastfeeding cessation to allow for the development of HIV antibodies. 11. For infants under 18 months of age, a positive antibody test requires NAT to confirm infection. 12. For infants older than 18 months, a negative antibody test confirms the infant is uninfected, while a positive antibody test confirms infection. 13. The WHO 2015 guidelines recommend that all pregnant and breastfeeding women with HIV initiate and continue ART as lifelong treatment. 14. Countries transitioning to this approach or expanding their programs may find the readiness assessment checklist useful, addressing issues from national policy to facility readiness. 15. The checklist and discussion guide were developed by the United States President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief and are part of the Interagency Task Team toolkit for managing the transition to Option B/B+ for pregnant women living with HIV. 16. Clinical staging for children younger than 15 years should be used, as adolescents are defined as 15 years or older. 17. Moderate malnutrition in children under 5 years is defined as weight-for-height < -2 z-score or mid-upper arm circumference ≥ 115 mm to < 125 mm. 18. Severe wasting in children under 5 years is defined as weight-for-height < -3 z-score, stunting as length-for-age/height-for-age < -2 z-score, and severe acute malnutrition as weight-for-height < -3 z-score, mid-upper arm circumference < 115 mm, or the presence of edema. 19. Some additional conditions may be included in regional classifications, such as penicilliosis in Asia, HIV-associated rectovaginal fistula in southern Africa, and reactivation of trypanosomiasis in Latin America. 20. For infants weighing less than 2000 g and older than 35 weeks of gestational age, the suggested doses are NVP 2 mg/kg per dose once daily and AZT 4 mg/kg per dose twice daily. 21. Simplified weight-based dosing for antiretroviral (ARV) formulations for infants and children has been developed to ensure accurate and safe administration. 22. Fixed-dose combinations are preferred for any regimen if available, and oral liquid or syrup formulations should be avoided where possible. Dispersible tablets are the preferred solid oral dosage forms. 23. Dosing for postnatal prophylaxis for HIV-exposed infants is not provided here but can be found in Annex 11, Section B. 24. The dosing guidance for newborns aligns with ongoing trials, and updates will be provided as trial results become available. 25. Reliable pharmacokinetic data in preterm infants are limited, and certain ARV drugs, such as LPV/r solution, should not be given to preterm infants until they reach 42 weeks of gestational age. 26. National program managers should ensure that products planned for use are currently available, of appropriate quality, and stable. 27. The simplified dosing schedule will be regularly reviewed and updated as additional data or newer formulations become available. 28. National programs are advised to consider the most recent product labeling for up-to-date information.
